messages.content: Write a post about starting a mentorship program on an engineering team. Around 250 words.

**We started a mentorship program. Here's what I got wrong.**

Six months ago our team had eleven engineers and one person who understood the billing service. When she took two weeks off, three tickets sat untouched. That was the argument for mentorship — not culture, not retention, just the fact that knowledge had pooled in one head.

So we paired people. Each pair got 45 minutes a week, on the calendar, protected. That's the whole design. No curriculum, no competency matrix, no quarterly rubric.

Pairing is where I went wrong. I matched by seniority, which sounds sensible and isn't. The pairs that worked were people on adjacent systems — the mentee already had questions, the mentor already had opinions. My most carefully senior match fizzled by week four because neither of them had anything concrete to talk about.

Second lesson: protect the time or skip the program. Two pairs let the meeting slide during a release crunch and never got it back. Now it's a recurring invite only the pair can cancel, and I ask about it in 1:1s.

What changed? Code review comments got longer and less defensive. Two engineers who'd never opened the billing service shipped changes to it. One mentee started mentoring a new hire, which I didn't plan and won't take credit for.

The failure mode isn't a bad program. It's an ambitious one — six pairs, a reading list, a tracking spreadsheet, dead by March.

Start smaller than feels worthwhile. Three pairs, one quarter. Then look at what actually happened.

**We started a mentorship program. Here's what I got wrong.**

Six months ago our team had eleven engineers and exactly one person who understood the billing service. She took two weeks off and three tickets sat there untouched. That was the case for mentorship — not culture, not retention, just the fact that all the knowledge about one system lived in a single head.

So we paired people up. Every pair got 45 minutes a week, on the calendar, protected. That's the entire design. No curriculum, no competency matrix, no quarterly rubric.

The pairing is where I got it wrong. I matched on seniority, which sounds reasonable and isn't. The pairs that took off were people working on neighboring systems — the mentee showed up with questions, the mentor showed up with opinions. My most deliberately senior match died by week four because neither of them had anything specific to say to each other.

Second lesson: defend the time or don't bother. Two pairs let the meeting slip during a release crunch and never recovered it. Now it's a recurring invite that only the pair can cancel, and I ask about it in 1:1s.

What came of it? Code review comments got longer and less defensive. Two engineers who'd never touched the billing service shipped changes to it. One mentee started mentoring a new hire, which I didn't plan and won't claim credit for.

The way these die isn't badly. It's ambitiously — six pairs, a reading list, a tracking spreadsheet, gone by March.

Start smaller than seems worth doing. Three pairs, one quarter. Then see what actually happened.
